海號琴為中世紀至文藝復興歐洲使用的弦鳴樂器，十五世紀在英格蘭流行，並延續至十八世: The tromba marina is a chordophone used in Europe from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance; it was popular in England in the fifteenth century and lasted into the eighteenth. Praetorius recorded its dimensions in 1618. When the trumpet was favoured in German churches, nuns who were not allowed to blow one took up this instrument instead, which is why it is called the “nun's fiddle”. The French royal stables band already had five trombe marine and crumhorns in 1662 and six in 1666. In the first half of the eighteenth century it fell out of common use and was found instead among travelling and street musicians. Ensembles still play it regularly today.

It was found in medieval and Renaissance Europe, popular in fifteenth-century England and still present in the eighteenth century; in German churches nuns used it because they were not allowed to blow the trumpet; the French royal stables band had five trombe marine and crumhorns in 1662 and six in 1666; after the first half of the eighteenth century it was mostly heard among travelling and street musicians, and playing groups use it today as well.
海號琴音色獨特而刺激，具有明亮銳利的質感，帶有強烈的鼻音特徵，如同小號的嘹亮音質: The tromba marina's timbre is distinctive and startling: bright and sharp, with a strong nasal quality, like the brilliance of a trumpet. Its range is wide, up to three or four octaves, and it is especially strong in the upper-middle register. Because it has a single string and is bowed, it has the flow of a string instrument yet the penetration and brilliance of brass. Its way of resonating is unusual: the tapered body and the resonating string produce a complex set of overtones, a reverberation with a metallic quality. Compared with the warm, heavy violin, the tromba marina sounds sharper and more startling; compared with a real trumpet it lacks weight but has more of the soft flexibility of strings. This special sound makes it highly expressive in Renaissance music.

The tromba marina is a triangular bowed instrument of medieval and Renaissance Europe, a chordophone, H-S number 321.321-71. Body and neck form a truncated cone, set on a triangular base, usually four to seven feet long, mostly with a single string though some carry resonating strings. It is not stopped: the thumb touches the nodes to sound the natural harmonics. Its bridge is unusual: one foot presses on the string and the other vibrates freely on an ivory or glass plate, producing a brassy buzzing sound close to a trumpet. In German churches nuns used it in place of the trumpet, which women were not allowed to play; after the first half of the eighteenth century it was seen only among travelling and street players.
琴身有兩種來源所述構造：三片木側板接成長三角形，或三至六片肋板配前面板；底部多開: The source describes two kinds of body: three wooden sides joined into an elongated triangle, or three to six ribs with a front plate; the bottom is mostly open and some have soundholes. The sounding string is generally the D string of a cello, but the source does not state the material. One foot of the bridge stands on an ivory or glass plate and the other vibrates freely; the guiding string is a second string wound on a peg. The materials of the pegs, the bridge itself, the ribs, the front plate and the neck are not stated.

The left hand stops the string, or changes the sounding length, to control pitch, and the right hand sets the string vibrating. A chordophone works by the vibration of the string being amplified through a resonating body. Draw the bow evenly and use the weight of the arm rather than the strength of the wrist.
